candidates.title: Transfer an uncaged HSR12X LM block onto a removing/mounting jig
candidates.objective: Bimanually butt a representative removing/mounting jig against an HSR12X rail, maintain parallel continuous support, and slide the uncaged recirculating-ball block fully onto the jig without losing a ball or contaminating or damaging the guide.
candidates.success_conditions: Full success requires physical end-face contact, parallel rail and jig axes, complete block transfer, all initially present balls still contained in four circulating rows, no impact, drop, contamination-zone contact, or unsafe inclination, and a stable one-second release. Safe jig mating and partial transfer may receive partial credit. Any lost ball, block jam, separated support interface, direct pose or velocity write, hidden weld, fixed ball, or collision suppression invalidates full success.
candidates.industrial_value: THK’s maintenance instructions prescribe a removing/mounting jig when block removal is unavoidable and require discontinuing use if a rolling element falls out. This makes preservation of the bearing elements an actual service outcome rather than an invented difficulty.
candidates.dexterity: One hand must keep a narrow jig physically butted and parallel to the rail while the other advances a small bearing block. The robot must regulate contact and regrasp without opening a gap that lets any freely simulated ball escape.

candidates.asset_plan: Author a representative full-scale HSR12XRM fixture using the visually verified A1-194/A1-195 drawings: 20 mm block height, 27 mm block width, 45 mm block length, 12 mm rail width, 11 mm rail height, and the documented four-row cross-section with end returns. Model every ball as an independent rigid PhysX body and preserve four physical circulation paths. Make the jig’s support cross-section continuous with the rail and clearly label its unpublished length, ball diameter/count, groove clearance, maximum transfer gap, and angular tolerance as prototype assumptions rather than THK specifications. Freeze those values before development and test ball circulation and loss, gap and inclination sensitivity, timestep stability, contact-force limits, reset freshness, and deliberate misalignment failures before YAM integration.
candidates.risk: The manufacturer drawings establish the selected model’s exterior, rail cross-section, four raceway rows, circulation through end plates, and lack of retention. Exact ball diameter/count, internal groove microprofile, jig length, and service tolerances are unpublished; these are bounded representative modeling assumptions requiring sensitivity tests and must not be presented as an exact THK replica.

candidates.title: Replace an industrial-robot External DressPack arm section
candidates.objective: Support a cable-and-hose bundle, release its clamps and adjustable bracket, remove the section without snagging or over-bending it, route a replacement along the lower and upper robot arms, and restore physical clamp capture and usable free length.
candidates.success_conditions: Full success requires every modeled clamp to be physically reopened and relatched, the bundle to follow the documented arm route, and its free length and bend state to remain within source-grounded limits. Hose escape, kink, excessive bend, connector impact, dropped bundle, false closure, or direct state manipulation scores zero.
candidates.industrial_value: ABB states that its clamps support quick, accurate replacement of the complete package to minimize production stoppage and reports that changing a DressPack section takes less than 30 minutes.
candidates.dexterity: The operation combines compliant bundle support, multiple latch operations, routing, regrasping, and length adjustment rather than simple cable transport.

evidence.locator: ABB External DressPack, “Easy replacement of upper and lower arm DressPack”

candidates.title: Install paired 2U ReadyRails and load a rack system through the locking transition
candidates.objective: Seat and latch both rails at the rack posts, extend their inner members, bimanually tilt and align a representative 2U system so its rear mounting nuts enter first, lower it into paired capture, release both locks, and slide the supported system into the rack.
skills: bimanual leveling of a rigid load
candidates.success_conditions: Full success requires all four rail ends physically seated and latched, rear mounting nuts captured before lowering, all remaining nuts retained, both inner-member locks released, and the system fully inserted and stable. Rail skew, false latch closure, one-sided loading, equipment drop, rack collision, bypassed clips, or direct state manipulation scores zero.
candidates.industrial_value: Dell’s official installation video documents the ReadyRails installation and loading sequence, including latch verification, rear-first mounting-nut engagement, lowering, lock release, and final insertion.
candidates.dexterity: The robot must register two rails independently, then support, level, tilt, and capture a large rigid load on two narrow telescoping members before coordinating lock release.

candidates.asset_plan: Acquire the matching Rack Installation Guide or public mechanical drawings and independently verify the relevant video frames. Build a representative rigid fixture with physical rack-post hooks, latches, telescoping members, mounting nuts, capture slots, and release clips. Test rail skew, one-sided capture, latch preload, center-of-mass sensitivity, clip timing, reach, and reset behavior in native PhysX.
candidates.risk: The transcript proves the procedure but does not reveal the essential hook, latch, nut-slot, telescoping-lock, rack-hole, or release-clip geometry. Workspace reach and safe load scaling also remain unverified.
missing_evidence: matching ReadyRails model and Rack Installation Guide
system mounting-nut and rail capture-slot dimensions
inner-member lock and metal release-clip mechanism
verified rack spacing, rail travel, equipment envelope, mass, and center of mass
pinned-YAM reach and safe scale study

selection_reason: The newly acquired and visually inspected THK HSR catalog resolves the prior ambiguous-selection failure: it identifies HSR12X as an unretained-ball model, establishes four circulating raceway rows, and supplies a consistent model-specific exterior and rail cross-section. Together with THK’s mandatory full-contact, parallel-jig procedure and explicit lost-ball rejection rule, this is sufficient for a mechanically faithful representative rigid-PhysX build. Its unpublished microgeometry is nonessential manufacturer calibration that can be disclosed, frozen, and sensitivity-tested. The ABB alternative still depends on unvalidated deformable physics and unknown latch geometry, while the Dell alternative lacks essential retention and capture geometry.
